title: Rumi and the reed
intro: The Masnavi of Rumi – some 26,000 couplets of stories, jokes and teaching – begins with a reed flute complaining that it has been cut from its reed-bed. These opening lines, the 'Song of the Reed', are the most famous verses of Persian mysticism. In this lesson you read all eighteen couplets, retell them in modern Persian, learn the words Sufis use for exile and return, see how a masnavi rhymes, and follow Rumi's life from Khorasan to Konya.
goals: read the eighteen couplets of the Song of the Reed and retell each one in modern Persian
use the vocabulary of longing and return: عشق، فراق، وصل، نیستان، اصل، سینه، شرحه شرحه
recognise the masnavi form – a new rhyme in every couplet – and hear its swinging metre
tell the story of Rumi's life and of his meeting with Shams of Tabriz

sections.title: The Song of the Reed
sections.intro: The opening of the Masnavi, couplet by couplet. From the second couplet on, the reed itself is speaking. Read each line aloud – the metre is easy to feel – and then look at the notes.

sentences.fa: بشنو این نی چون شکایت می‌کند / از جدایی‌ها حکایت می‌کند
sentences.r: beshnow in ney chon shekāyat mi-konad / az jodāyi-hā hekāyat mi-konad
sentences.en: Listen to this reed, how it complains: it is telling a tale of separations.
sentences.note: Many Iranians know the line as «بشنو از نی چون حکایت می‌کند / از جدایی‌ها شکایت می‌کند» – 'Listen to the reed as it tells its tale: it complains of separations.' Editions based on the oldest manuscripts have the words given here. [[بشنو|beshnow]] = [[گوش کن|gush kon]] 'listen'.

sentences.fa: کز نیستان تا مرا ببریده‌اند / در نفیرم مرد و زن نالیده‌اند
sentences.r: k-az neyestān tā marā bebride-and / dar nafir-am mard o zan nālide-and
sentences.en: 'Ever since they cut me from the reed-bed, men and women have wept at my cry.'
sentences.note: From here on the reed speaks. [[کز|kaz]] = [[که از|ke az]]; [[تا|tā]] here means 'ever since'. [[نفیر|nafir]] is a loud, wailing cry.

sentences.fa: سینه خواهم شرحه شرحه از فراق / تا بگویم شرح درد اشتیاق
sentences.r: sine khāham sharhe sharhe az farāgh / tā beguyam sharh-e dard-e eshtiyāgh
sentences.en: 'I want a breast torn to shreds by separation, so that I can tell it the pain of longing.'
sentences.note: [[شرحه شرحه|sharhe sharhe]] 'cut into strips' plays on [[شرح|sharh]] 'explanation': only a torn heart can understand longing. [[خواهم|khāham]] = [[می‌خواهم|mi-khāham]].

sentences.fa: هر کسی کو دور ماند از اصل خویش / باز جوید روزگار وصل خویش
sentences.r: har kas-i k-u dur mānd az asl-e khish / bāz juyad ruzgār-e vasl-e khish
sentences.en: 'Whoever is left far from his origin seeks once more the time when he was one with it.'
sentences.note: [[کو|ku]] = [[که او|ke u]]; [[خویش|khish]] = [[خود|khod]]; [[جوید|juyad]] = [[می‌جوید|mi-juyad]] 'seeks'. This couplet is the key to the whole Masnavi: everything comes from God and longs to go back.

sentences.fa: من به هر جمعیتی نالان شدم / جفت بدحالان و خوش‌حالان شدم
sentences.r: man be har jam'iyyat-i nālān shodam / joft-e bad-hālān o khosh-hālān shodam
sentences.en: 'In every gathering I have wept; I have kept company with the unhappy and the happy alike.'
sentences.note: [[جمعیت|jam'iyyat]] here is 'a gathering', not 'population'; [[جفت|joft]] is 'a pair, a companion'.

sentences.fa: هر کسی از ظن خود شد یار من / از درون من نجست اسرار من
sentences.r: har kas-i az zann-e khod shod yār-e man / az darun-e man najost asrār-e man
sentences.en: 'Each one became my friend from his own guess; none of them looked for my secrets within me.'
sentences.note: [[ظن|zann]] 'supposition, guess'. [[نجست|najost]] is the past of [[جستن|jostan]] 'to seek'. People enjoyed the music without asking what it meant.

sentences.fa: سر من از ناله‌ی من دور نیست / لیک چشم و گوش را آن نور نیست
sentences.r: serr-e man az nāle-ye man dur nist / lik cheshm o gush rā ān nur nist
sentences.en: 'My secret is not far from my lament, but eye and ear do not have the light to see it.'
sentences.note: [[سر|serr]], with a doubled r, is 'secret' – not [[سر|sar]] 'head'. [[لیک|lik]] = [[ولی|vali]]. In [[چشم و گوش را … نیست|cheshm o gush rā … nist]] 'eye and ear do not have', را means 'for'.

sentences.fa: تن ز جان و جان ز تن مستور نیست / لیک کس را دید جان دستور نیست
sentences.r: tan ze jān o jān ze tan mastur nist / lik kas rā did-e jān dastur nist
sentences.en: 'Body is not veiled from soul, nor soul from body – yet no one is permitted to see the soul.'
sentences.note: [[مستور|mastur]] 'veiled, hidden'. [[دستور|dastur]] meant 'permission'; today it means 'order' or 'grammar'.

sentences.fa: آتش است این بانگ نای و نیست باد / هر که این آتش ندارد نیست باد
sentences.r: ātash ast in bāng-e nāy o nist bād / har ke in ātash nadārad nist bād
sentences.en: 'This cry of the reed is fire, not wind – and whoever does not have this fire, may he be nothing!'
sentences.note: A pun: [[نیست باد|nist bād]] first means 'it is not wind', then 'may he be nothing' – [[باد|bād]] is also the old wish form of بودن, 'may it be'. [[نای|nāy]] is another form of [[نی|ney]].

sentences.fa: آتش عشق است کاندر نی فتاد / جوشش عشق است کاندر می فتاد
sentences.r: ātash-e eshgh ast k-andar ney fetād / jushesh-e eshgh ast k-andar mey fetād
sentences.en: 'It is the fire of love that has fallen into the reed; it is the ferment of love that has fallen into the wine.'
sentences.note: [[کاندر|kāndar]] = [[که اندر|ke andar]], and [[اندر|andar]] is the old [[در|dar]] 'in'; [[فتاد|fetād]] = [[افتاد|oftād]]. Love is what makes the reed sing and the wine ferment.

sentences.fa: نی حریف هر که از یاری برید / پرده‌هایش پرده‌های ما درید
sentences.r: ney harif-e har ke az yār-i borid / parde-hā-yash parde-hā-ye mā darid
sentences.en: 'The reed is the companion of all who have been cut off from a friend; its melodies have torn our veils.'
sentences.note: [[حریف|harif]] was a 'companion' (today it means 'rival'). [[پرده|parde]] is both a musical mode and a veil: the reed's melodies tear away what hides us.

sentences.fa: همچو نی زهری و تریاقی که دید / همچو نی دمساز و مشتاقی که دید
sentences.r: hamcho ney zahr-i o taryāgh-i ke did / hamcho ney damsāz o moshtāgh-i ke did
sentences.en: 'Who has ever seen a poison and an antidote like the reed? Who has seen a companion and a lover like the reed?'
sentences.note: [[همچو|hamcho]] = [[مثل|mesl-e]] 'like'; [[که دید؟|ke did?]] 'who has seen?' means 'no one'. The reed wounds with longing and heals with it.

sentences.fa: نی حدیث راه پرخون می‌کند / قصه‌های عشق مجنون می‌کند
sentences.r: ney hadis-e rāh-e porkhun mi-konad / ghesse-hā-ye eshgh-e Majnun mi-konad
sentences.en: 'The reed tells of a road soaked in blood; it tells the stories of Majnun's love.'
sentences.note: [[مجنون|Majnun]], 'the madman', is the lover of Leyli in the best-known love story of the Islamic world.

sentences.fa: محرم این هوش جز بی‌هوش نیست / مر زبان را مشتری جز گوش نیست
sentences.r: mahram-e in hush joz bi-hush nist / mar zabān rā moshtari joz gush nist
sentences.en: 'None but the senseless may enter this sense, as the tongue has no customer but the ear.'
sentences.note: A [[محرم|mahram]] is someone close enough to be let into the private part of a house. Only one who is 'out of his mind' ([[بی‌هوش|bi-hush]]) can enter this kind of mind. [[مر زبان را|mar zabān rā]] = [[زبان را|zabān rā]] 'for the tongue'.

sentences.fa: در غم ما روزها بیگاه شد / روزها با سوزها همراه شد
sentences.r: dar gham-e mā ruz-hā bigāh shod / ruz-hā bā suz-hā hamrāh shod
sentences.en: 'In our grief the days have grown late; the days have walked hand in hand with burning pains.'

sentences.fa: روزها گر رفت گو رو باک نیست / تو بمان ای آن که چون تو پاک نیست
sentences.r: ruz-hā gar raft gu row bāk nist / to bemān ey ān ke chon to pāk nist
sentences.en: 'If the days are gone, say: let them go, no matter – but you, stay, you who have no equal in purity.'
sentences.note: [[گو|gu]] = [[بگو|begu]], [[رو|row]] = [[برو|borow]], [[باک نیست|bāk nist]] 'there is no fear' – 'never mind'. The 'you' who must stay is love itself.

sentences.fa: هر که جز ماهی ز آبش سیر شد / هر که بی‌روزی است روزش دیر شد
sentences.r: har ke joz māhi ze āb-ash sir shod / har ke bi-ruzi ast ruz-ash dir shod
sentences.en: 'All but the fish have had their fill of water; for whoever lacks his daily bread, the day drags on.'
sentences.note: The fish – the lover – can never have enough water – love. [[روزی|ruzi]] is one's daily bread, the share God gives.

questions.q: What is the reed complaining about?
options: that it has been cut from the reed-bed
that nobody plays it any more
that it is made of poison

questions.q: What kind of listener does the reed want?
options: one whose breast has been torn by separation
one who knows the theory of music

sections.title: A poem in rhyming couplets
sections.md:
The passage ends with a couplet that closes the door on explanation: [[در نیابد حال پخته هیچ خام / پس سخن کوتاه باید والسلام|dar nayābad hāl-e pokhte hich khām / pas sokhan kutāh bāyad vassalām|no one raw can grasp the state of the ripe – so the words must be short, and farewell]]. [[والسلام|vassalām]], Arabic for 'and peace', is how you end a letter – or an argument.

**A poem in pairs.** The **masnavi** ([[مثنوی|masnavi]]) – the word means 'in pairs' – is the Persian form for long poems. Unlike the ghazal, which keeps one rhyme from beginning to end, a masnavi gives **every couplet its own rhyme**: the two halves of each line rhyme with each other, and the next couplet starts afresh (*aa bb cc…*). Look at the first lines: [[شکایت|shekāyat]] / [[حکایت|hekāyat]], [[ببریده‌اند|bebride-and]] / [[نالیده‌اند|nālide-and]], [[فراق|farāgh]] / [[اشتیاق|eshtiyāgh]]. Because the poet never runs out of rhymes this way, a masnavi can go on for as long as the story needs: Ferdowsi's *Shahnameh*, Nezami's romances and Attar's *Conference of the Birds* are all masnavis.

**The Masnavi.** Rumi's poem is simply called *the* Masnavi, or [[مثنوی معنوی|masnavi-ye ma'navi]], 'the masnavi of inner meaning'. Its six books ([[دفتر|daftar]]) hold some 26,000 couplets of stories, jokes, sermons and prayers, all in the same light, swinging metre, *ramal*: DUM-da-DUM-DUM, DUM-da-DUM-DUM, DUM-da-DUM – [[بشنو این نی چون شکایت می‌کند|beshnow in ney chon shekāyat mi-konad]]. Rumi composed it aloud over many years, and his disciple Hosam al-Din Chalabi wrote it down.

**The reed.** The first eighteen couplets, the **Song of the Reed** ([[نی‌نامه|ney-nāme]]), are the overture. A reed is cut from the reed-bed, hollowed, pierced and played – and everything it plays is a lament for home. The reed is the human soul, cut off from its origin in God; its music is our longing; the breath that makes it sing is love. Whoever hears the song with a torn breast understands. The rest, Rumi says at the end, are 'raw', and with them the talk must be short.

ex.en: The sound of the ney is sad.

items.note: plural [[اسرار|asrār]]. Not to be confused with [[سر|sar]] 'head'.

sections.title: The song in modern Persian: couplets 1–9
sections.md:
Rumi's Persian is a century older than Hafez's, but the method is the same: put the verb last, open the contractions, replace the old words. Rumi adds a favourite of his own, **the pun**: [[شرحه|sharhe]] 'a strip of flesh' and [[شرح|sharh]] 'explanation'; [[نیست باد|nist bād]] 'it is not wind' and 'may he be nothing'; [[پرده|parde]] 'a musical mode' and 'a veil'. A paraphrase has to choose one meaning – which is why Iranians always go back to the original.

Here are the hardest phrases of the first nine couplets, and below them each couplet in plain modern Persian.

examples.r: har kas bā gomān-e khod-ash dust-e man shod, vali kas-i be donbāl-e rāz-hā-ye darun-e man na-gasht.
examples.en: Couplet 6: Everyone became my friend according to his own idea of me, but no one looked for the secrets inside me.

examples.fa: راز من از ناله‌ام جدا نیست، اما چشم و گوش آن نور را ندارند که آن را ببینند.
examples.r: rāz-e man az nāle-am jodā nist, ammā cheshm o gush ān nur rā nadārand ke ān rā bebinand.
examples.en: Couplet 7: My secret is not separate from my lament, but eye and ear do not have the light to see it.

examples.fa: تن از جان و جان از تن پنهان نیست، اما به هیچ کس اجازه نداده‌اند که جان را ببیند.
examples.r: tan az jān o jān az tan penhān nist, ammā be hich kas ejāze na-dāde-and ke jān rā bebinad.
examples.en: Couplet 8: The body is not hidden from the soul nor the soul from the body, but no one has been allowed to see the soul.

examples.fa: صدای نی آتش است، نه باد؛ هر کس این آتش را ندارد، بهتر است نباشد.
examples.r: sedā-ye ney ātash ast, na bād; har kas in ātash rā nadārad, behtar ast na-bāshad.
examples.en: Couplet 9: The sound of the reed is fire, not wind; whoever does not have this fire had better not exist.

sections.title: Couplets 10–18 in modern Persian
sections.md:
In the second half of the passage, watch for three old forms that come back in lesson 4: [[اندر|andar]] for [[در|dar]] (in [[کاندر|kāndar]] = [[که اندر|ke andar]]); [[مر … را|mar … rā]] wrapped around an object; and short imperatives without be-: [[گو|gu]] 'say', [[رو|row]] 'go'.

Two everyday words began as metaphors like Rumi's and are still alive: [[خام|khām]] 'raw' and [[پخته|pokhte]] 'cooked'. You can call an inexperienced colleague [[خام|khām]], and say of someone who has grown wiser [[پخته شده است|pokhte shode ast]].

examples.en: Couplet 18: A raw person does not understand the state of a ripe one, so the talk must be cut short – and that is all.

sections.title: The words of longing
sections.md:
The opening of the Masnavi gave Persian a whole vocabulary of longing. Most of these words are ordinary – [[سینه|sine]] is just 'chest', [[اصل|asl]] 'origin, root' – but since Rumi they also tell the story of the soul. Cut from its **reed-bed** ([[نیستان|neyestān]]), the soul lives in **separation** ([[فراق|farāgh]], [[هجران|hejrān]], [[جدایی|jodāyi]]) and longs for **union** ([[وصل|vasl]], [[وصال|vesāl]]) with its **origin** ([[اصل|asl]]). Only **love** ([[عشق|eshgh]]) can carry it back, and only a **torn breast** ([[سینه‌ی شرحه شرحه|sine-ye sharhe sharhe]]) understands the song.

You will hear these words far outside poetry: in pop songs, in letters between lovers, in the speech of Iranians abroad talking about home.

sections.title: Rumi: from Khorasan to Konya
sections.intro: The life of the poet in modern written Persian. Notice the past tenses of narration and the many names: Iranians call him Mowlana ('our master') or Mowlavi; the West calls him Rumi.

sentences.fa: جلال‌الدین محمد بلخی، که ایرانیان او را «مولانا» یا «مولوی» می‌نامند، در سال ۶۰۴ هجری قمری در خراسان بزرگ به دنیا آمد.
sentences.r: Jalāl-od-din Mohammad-e Balkhi, ke irāniyān u rā «Mowlānā» yā «Mowlavi» mi-nāmand, dar sāl-e sheshsad-o-chahār-e hejri-ye ghamari dar Khorāsān-e bozorg be donyā āmad.
sentences.en: Jalal al-Din Mohammad Balkhi, whom Iranians call 'Mowlana' or 'Mowlavi', was born in Greater Khorasan in the year 604 of the Hijra (1207).

sentences.fa: در غرب او را «رومی» می‌شناسند، چون بیشتر عمرش را در آناتولی، یعنی سرزمین «روم»، گذراند.
sentences.r: dar gharb u rā «Rumi» mi-shenāsand, chon bishtar-e omr-ash rā dar Ānātoli, ya'ni sarzamin-e «Rum», gozarānd.
sentences.en: In the West he is known as 'Rumi', because he spent most of his life in Anatolia, the land of 'Rum'.

sections.title: The reed flute and the turning dervishes
sections.md:
**The ney.** The Persian [[نی|ney]] is nothing but a length of reed with six finger holes, yet its breathy, almost human voice is the sound of Persian classical music – and of mourning. Because of Rumi, every ney player is also, a little, playing the Song of the Reed: concerts often begin with a ney solo, and singers set its couplets to music.

**Sama'.** Rumi loved music and the turning dance. After his death his followers, the Mevlevi order, made it into a ceremony, the [[سماع|samā']]: dervishes in white robes and tall felt hats turn slowly, the right hand raised to receive grace from heaven, the left lowered to pass it on to the earth, while the ney plays. In Konya the anniversary of Rumi's death, 17 December, is celebrated as his 'wedding night' ([[شب عروس|shab-e arus]]) – the night he was united with God.

**Whose poet?** Rumi was born in Khorasan, wrote in Persian and lived in Anatolia, so Afghanistan, Iran, Tajikistan and Turkey all call him their own. Iranians call him [[مولانا|Mowlānā]] 'our master' or [[مولوی|Mowlavi]]; Turks say *Mevlânâ*. In Iran the Song of the Reed is learned at school, and [[هر کسی کو دور ماند از اصل خویش|har kas-i k-u dur mānd az asl-e khish]] is the line people reach for when they talk about exile and homesickness.

sections.title: Tips
items: Read the Song of the Reed with its metre: DUM-da-DUM-DUM, DUM-da-DUM-DUM, DUM-da-DUM. The beat tells you to read ماند in couplet 4 as one syllable, *mānd*, and بشنو as *besh-now*.
In Rumi, ز، کز، کو، کاندر are contractions: از، که از، که او، که اندر.

Some words have moved on since the 13th century: حریف 'companion' → 'rival', دستور 'permission' → 'order, grammar', جمعیت 'gathering' → 'population'. Ask yourself whether a word you know meant something else then.
سر is two words: *sar* 'head' and *serr* 'secret' (plural اسرار). In poetry about love, it is usually the secret.
خام and پخته are useful today: آدم خامی است 'he is naive', خیلی پخته شده 'she has really matured'.
Most Iranians quote the popular first line, «بشنو از نی چون حکایت می‌کند / از جدایی‌ها شکایت می‌کند». Recognise both versions – and don't correct anyone.
